newsitem.title: USA: NYPA proposes open power transmission rate plan.
newsitem.headline: NYPA proposes open power transmission rate plan.

text.p: The New York Power Authority (NYPA) outlined a rate plan for use of its transmission lines that would accomodate the opening of the nation's power grid to competing wholesale electricity suppliers.
"We believe in open access and we believe all transmission owners must participate actively to bring its full benefits to consumers," said NYPA chief executive officer C.D. Rappleyea in a statement.
Current and new NYPA transmission customers served by a single line would see no increase in transmission rates, the utility said.
The proposal also included a "rolled-in" rate for customers who receive power over more than one NYPA transmission line, it said.
The new rolled-in rate would affect relatively few customers and increase their overall electricity bills by less than one percent, NYPA said.

NYPA's trustees on Tuesday gave preliminary approval to an initial rolled-in rate of $2.23 a kilowatt-month (kw-month) for firm service on multiple segments of the utility's transmission network, replacing the current rate of $2.19, it said.
The new rate reflects the overall costs of NYPA's integrated transmission system, as required by Federal Energy Regulatory Commission methodology, the utility said.

NYPA said its trustees also proposed keeping its current firm rates for single transmission lines. These include charges of $1.60 per kw-month for service on a line from Massena to Marcy, near Utica; $1.60 for service from Marcy to East Fishkill in Dutchess County; and $1.30 for lines carrying electricity from the St Lawrence-Franklin D Roosevelt and Niagara hydroelectric projects.
The rate for non-firm, or interruptible, transmission would be pegged to the new firm rolled-in rate and would not exceed charges for an equivalent amount of firm service.
Following additional customer meetings and a public forum Nov 14 in New York City, the trustees would take final action on the proposed open access tariffs, NYPA said.
The utility said it expected to file these transmission tariffs with FERC by the end of 1996.
NYPA noted it continued to discuss with the seven investor-owned utility members of the New York Power Pool on a single statewide transmission tariff that could supplant its own proposed tariff.

Earlier this year, FERC directed the nation's electric utilities to open their transmission lines to competing electricity suppliers to promote competition, boost efficiency and reduce costs for consumers.
NYPA, a state-owned power agency, supplies a fourth of the New York's electricity.
